\label{ch:guardar-y-dejar}
\hlchaptermodality{383}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say guardar, dejar, sacar and buscar, and name four everyday actions.}

\section[guardar]{guardar — why English has both ward and guard}

\label{lesson:ES-C383-guardar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to pay}, then \emph{to stay}. (\emph{Pagar}; \emph{quedar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la llave — something you keep.
  \item la casa — where you keep it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guar-DAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. \emph{Gu-} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{g} followed by a real \emph{w} glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{guardar} — \textquotedblleft{}to keep, to put away.\textquotedblright{}

This one is not Latin. It comes from a Germanic verb \textbf{wardōn}, to watch over — the same root as English \textbf{ward}, in the sense of watching and protecting.

The interesting part is the first sound. Latin and its descendants had no \textbf{w-} at the start of a word, so when Germanic words arrived, Romance speakers reached for the nearest thing they had and produced \textbf{gu-}. \emph{Wardōn} became \emph{guardar}.

Now watch what that does to English, which borrowed from both sides.

English already had \textbf{ward} from its own Germanic stock. Then it borrowed the French version of the very same word and got \textbf{guard}. Both are in the dictionary, meaning almost the same thing, and most speakers never notice.

The pattern repeats down the whole family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{warden} and a \textbf{guardian}
  \item a \textbf{reward} and a \textbf{regard}
  \item \textbf{warranty} and \textbf{guarantee}
  \item and the names \textbf{William} and \textbf{Guillermo}, which are one name
\end{itemize}

Each pair is one word that entered English twice, once before the sound change and once after. Whenever you meet an English pair where one has \emph{w-} and the other \emph{gu-}, you are looking at this.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{guardar}. And you can spot a \emph{w-}/\emph{gu-} pair on sight.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guardar}
  \item \emph{guardar la llave}
  \item \emph{guardar en casa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Spanish have \emph{gu-} where Germanic had \emph{w-}? (Romance had no word-initial \emph{w-}.) Name a pair. (\emph{Ward} and \emph{guard}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dejar]{dejar — the d- was borrowed from another verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C383-dejar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to stay}, then \emph{to keep}. (\emph{Quedar}; \emph{guardar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la puerta — something you leave open.
  \item guardar — the opposite move.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de-JAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is the rasping sound made at the back of the mouth, not an English \emph{j}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to leave, to let.\textquotedblright{}

The root is Latin \textbf{laxare}, to loosen or slacken, from \emph{laxus}, loose. Leaving something alone is loosening your grip on it, and letting somebody do something is slackening the rein.

But \emph{laxare} does not give you \emph{dejar}, and the gap is the lesson. Latin \emph{l-} gives Spanish \emph{l-}, and older Spanish had exactly what you would predict: \textbf{lejar}. That form is written down.

So where did the \emph{d-} come from? The Academy's dictionary answers it in three words — \emph{infl. por dar}. \textbf{Dar}, to give, is one of the commonest verbs in the language, and it sat close to \emph{lejar} in meaning and in use. Its opening consonant leaked across. The word was pulled out of shape by a neighbour.

That kind of change has no rule behind it. It happens because two words keep company, and it is worth seeing once, because a sound law would never have predicted this \emph{d}.

English took \emph{laxare} several times: \textbf{relax}, \textbf{lax}, and — through French — \textbf{leash}, which is a thing you slacken. \textbf{Laxative} is the same idea applied somewhere else entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{dejar}. And you know one word can reshape another.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dejar}
  \item \emph{dejar la puerta}
  \item \emph{guardar y dejar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{laxare} mean? (To loosen.) And which verb lent \emph{dejar} its \emph{d-}? (\emph{Dar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sacar]{sacar — an argument that is still open}

\label{lesson:ES-C383-sacar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to keep}, then \emph{to leave}. (\emph{Guardar}; \emph{dejar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dinero — something you take out.
  \item dejar — a near neighbour in meaning.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sa-CAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sacar} — \textquotedblleft{}to take out.\textquotedblright{}

This is a word where the honest answer is that scholars disagree, and it is worth watching them disagree.

Start with what is settled — a negative. \emph{Sacar} is \textbf{not} a verb built on \textbf{saco}, a bag, in the plain way it looks like it might be. Making a verb from \emph{saco} would give you something meaning to put \emph{into} a sack, which is the opposite of what \emph{sacar} means. Corominas dismissed the attempt to rescue that reading as a desperate expedient.

From there the road forks.

Corominas proposed \textbf{Gothic sakan}, to go to law, to dispute — the idea being a legal one, taking something out by judgement. The Academy's dictionary follows him, with \emph{Quizá} in front of it.

A long line of Romance scholars prefers \textbf{Latin saccare}. That looks like the bag again, and it is not: alongside the bag, Latin \emph{saccus} named a \textbf{filter}, and the verb \emph{saccare} is written down only in the sense of filtering — straining wine, straining water. Taking out by filtering is a very different picture from taking out by lawsuit.

So the bag may be a distant relative after all, by way of a strainer rather than a sack. Nobody has closed the question. What you can say safely is the negative, and that \textbf{saquear}, to plunder, really does come from \emph{saco}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{sacar}. And you can hold two proposals without picking one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sacar}
  \item \emph{sacar el dinero}
  \item \emph{guardar y sacar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the settled part? (That \emph{sacar} is not a plain verb from \emph{saco}, a bag.) What did Latin \emph{saccus} mean besides a bag? (A filter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[buscar]{buscar — one of the commonest verbs, and nobody knows}

\label{lesson:ES-C383-buscar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to leave}, then \emph{to take out}. (\emph{Dejar}; \emph{sacar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la llave — something you look for.
  \item la calle — where you look.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bus-CAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The opening \emph{b} is soft between vowels and firmer at the start of a phrase. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{buscar} — \textquotedblleft{}to look for.\textquotedblright{}

Every lesson so far has ended somewhere. This one does not, and that is the point of it.

\emph{Buscar} is one of the most-used verbs in Spanish. It is written down in the eleventh century. And Corominas, whose dictionary is the standard work on Spanish origins, gives his verdict as \textbf{de origen desconocido} — of unknown origin. That is his strongest negative label, stronger than calling something uncertain.

He does float an idea. Perhaps, he asks, a Celtic word about winning or conquering? Then he answers his own question: the hypothesis, though possible, is very risky. Two modern dictionaries of reconstructed Celtic list what that root became in each language, and \emph{buscar} is on neither list.

There is a second story you may meet, connecting \emph{buscar} to \textbf{bosque}, a wood, as though searching were foraging. The dates refuse it. \emph{Bosque} does not appear in Castilian until the fifteenth century, four hundred years after \emph{buscar} is already in use. A word cannot descend from one that arrives later.

One relative can be pointed at, and it is English. To \textbf{busk} meant to go about seeking, and a \textbf{busker} — a street performer — is one who goes about seeking. The dictionaries name \emph{buscar} in that chain. It tells you nothing about where \emph{buscar} began, and it is the one thread that holds.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name four more everyday actions: \emph{guardar}, \emph{dejar}, \emph{sacar}, \emph{buscar}. Say which one you do most.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{buscar}
  \item \emph{buscar la llave}
  \item \emph{guardar, dejar, sacar, buscar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Corominas's verdict on \emph{buscar}? (Of unknown origin.) Why can it not come from \emph{bosque}? (\emph{Bosque} arrives four centuries later.)
\end{tcolorbox}
